question: I'm interested in the aquaculture industry, particularly the research being done into reducing the fishmeal in aquaculture diets. Get me the name of whichever one of its authors is listed as an author on the most other papers (from any publication, any time prior to June 2024). Please provide just the author's name.

# Effects of dietary tuna hydrolysate supplementation on feed intake, growth performance, feed utilization and health status of Asian sea bass (Lates calcarifer) fed a low fish meal soybean meal-based diet
### Abstract
This study aimed to examine the effects of dietary tuna hydrolysate supplementation on feed intake, growth, feed utilization and health status of Asian sea bass. Experimental diets included a high fish meal-based diet (HFM diet) containing 45% of fish meal, a low fish meal-based diet (LFM diet) in which 55% of fish meal protein was replaced with soybean meal and the LFM diet coated with 2.5% tuna hydrolysate (LFM + TH diet). Fish were fed diets for 8 weeks. Growth rate, feed intake, feed efficiency, protein efficiency ratio, nitrogen retention, intraperitoneal fat and serum albumin of fish-fed LFM + TH diet were significantly higher than those of fish-fed LFM diet (_p_< 0.05). No significant differences in carcass chemical compositions, serum cholesterol, triglyceride, aspartate aminotransferase, lysozyme activity, superoxide dismutase and trypsin and lipase activities were found in hepatopancreas and anterior intestine among the dietary treatments. Fish-fed LFM + TH diet displayed a longer length of distal intestine villi than those of fish-fed LFM + TH diet. No histopathological changes in the liver were observed in this study. The results suggest that dietary supplementation of 2.5% tuna hydrolysate is sufficient to enhance the diet palatability, which can increase the replacement levels of fish meal protein with soybean meal up to 55% in a low fish meal soybean meal-based diet without negative impacts on feed intake and growth performance of juvenile Asian sea bass.

# Effects of dietary tuna hydrolysate supplementation on feed intake, growth performance, feed utilization and health status of Asian sea bass (Lates calcarifer) fed a low fish meal soybean meal-based diet
### Abstract
This study aimed to examine the effects of dietary tuna hydrolysate supplementation on feed intake, growth, feed utilization and health status of Asian sea bass. Experimental diets included a high fish meal-based diet (HFM diet) containing 45% of fish meal, a low fish meal-based diet (LFM diet) in which 55% of fish meal protein was replaced with soybean meal and the LFM diet coated with 2.5% tuna hydrolysate (LFM + TH diet). Fish were fed diets for 8 weeks. Growth rate, feed intake, feed efficiency, protein efficiency ratio, nitrogen retention, intraperitoneal fat and serum albumin of fish-fed LFM + TH diet were significantly higher than those of fish-fed LFM diet (_p_< 0.05). No significant differences in carcass chemical compositions, serum cholesterol, triglyceride, aspartate aminotransferase, lysozyme activity, superoxide dismutase and trypsin and lipase activities were found in hepatopancreas and anterior intestine among the dietary treatments. Fish-fed LFM + TH diet displayed a longer length of distal intestine villi than those of fish-fed LFM + TH diet. No histopathological changes in the liver were observed in this study. The results suggest that dietary supplementation of 2.5% tuna hydrolysate is sufficient to enhance the diet palatability, which can increase the replacement levels of fish meal protein with soybean meal up to 55% in a low fish meal soybean meal-based diet without negative impacts on feed intake and growth performance of juvenile Asian sea bass.

# Effects of dietary tuna hydrolysate supplementation on feed intake, growth performance, feed utilization and health status of Asian sea bass (Lates calcarifer) fed a low fish meal soybean meal-based diet
### Abstract
This study aimed to examine the effects of dietary tuna hydrolysate supplementation on feed intake, growth, feed utilization and health status of Asian sea bass. Experimental diets included a high fish meal-based diet (HFM diet) containing 45% of fish meal, a low fish meal-based diet (LFM diet) in which 55% of fish meal protein was replaced with soybean meal and the LFM diet coated with 2.5% tuna hydrolysate (LFM + TH diet). Fish were fed diets for 8 weeks. Growth rate, feed intake, feed efficiency, protein efficiency ratio, nitrogen retention, intraperitoneal fat and serum albumin of fish-fed LFM + TH diet were significantly higher than those of fish-fed LFM diet (_p_< 0.05). No significant differences in carcass chemical compositions, serum cholesterol, triglyceride, aspartate aminotransferase, lysozyme activity, superoxide dismutase and trypsin and lipase activities were found in hepatopancreas and anterior intestine among the dietary treatments. Fish-fed LFM + TH diet displayed a longer length of distal intestine villi than those of fish-fed LFM + TH diet. No histopathological changes in the liver were observed in this study. The results suggest that dietary supplementation of 2.5% tuna hydrolysate is sufficient to enhance the diet palatability, which can increase the replacement levels of fish meal protein with soybean meal up to 55% in a low fish meal soybean meal-based diet without negative impacts on feed intake and growth performance of juvenile Asian sea bass.

## 1. Introduction
Concurrently, the European Fund for Maritime Affairs, Fisheries and Aquaculture (EMFF) (2021–2027) fosters initiatives that emphasise a sustainable approach to low-carbon emissions, the provision of clean and equitable energy, and the facilitation of green and blue investments for the promotion of a circular economy [29]. The implementation of circular practices in aquaculture has the potential to produce healthy, nutritious food that is cultivated in a controlled environment [24].
The scientific literature focuses on the benefits of recirculation systems, integrated systems and reuse of fish waste. A recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) involves the purification of wastewater from pollutants by recycling the water. In addition, the RASs can support the rearing of fish alongside other species that convert waste into nutrients, making the system more sustainable [30]. Integrated multitrophic aquaculture (IMTA) is a system that involves the use of organisms from different trophic levels. Waste produced by organisms at higher trophic levels (i.e., fish and molluscs) is used by organisms at lower trophic levels for sustenance, thereby acting as water biofilters [31]. Fish waste, including heads, tails, scales, bones, viscera (internal organs) and skin, are subjected to a silage process that transforms them into a hydrolysate rich in proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals and other nutrients easily assimilated by aquatic and terrestrial animals. In addition, the silage process is commonly carried out with low energy and labour efficiency, thus making the whole process sustainable [32,33,34,35]. Fish silage can be used as an alternative to conventional fertilisers due to its nutrient-rich composition, contributing to the reduction in environmental waste and pollution [35,36].

## 1. Introduction
To the best of our knowledge existent literature reviews include studies focusing on the bibliometric analysis of circular economy practices adopted in maritime processes and aquaculture. These studies report a system-wide (micro, meso and macro) classification of research and map literature and global trends using VOSWER, respectively [37,38,39]. Other studies [40,41] based on bibliometric analysis specifically focus on the sustainability of feed used in aquaculture and do not examine the specific circular and sustainable practices adopted in aquaculture. However, there is no existing literature that has conducted a scope analysis of studies undertaken in the aquaculture sector in the context of the circular economy over the last decade, identifying and describing the benefits and disadvantages of individual circular practices, their frequency of implementation, as well as network and clustering analysis. So, the aim of this study is to fill a gap in the literature on circularity practices in aquaculture, applying an innovative method of bibliometric analysis to identify the circular practices implemented in the aquaculture sector in detail.

## 1. Introduction
However, there is no extant literature that has conducted a scoping analysis of studies undertaken in the aquaculture sector in the context of the circular economy over the last decade. This study’s primary objective is to provide a comprehensive review of scientific articles on aquaculture and the circular economy published in the last ten years (2015–2025). Selected articles are described, and potential advantages and disadvantages of circularity practices are identified. The study aims to establish a framework for the recent literature on aquaculture and the circular economy. Specifically, it aims to detect research areas and techniques that can support scholars and companies in improving the sustainability of the aquaculture sector. In addition, this paper aims to provide aquaculture companies with an understanding of the main assessment tools used to measure the sustainability of aquaculture production processes. This study may also be of interest to researchers seeking to understand circularity trends over the last ten years. This will involve carrying out a measurement of the circular practices applied in the relevant studies. A bibliometric analysis was conducted to identify the salient points of this field of research and potential future developments. The frequency with which articles on the subject were published from 2015 to 2025 was analysed. The authors’ affiliations were then considered to understand the geographical distribution of the studies and the places where the experiments were conducted. Furthermore, VOSviewer (VoS) software (version 1.6.20) [42] was utilised to identify a network of recurring words in the abstracts of the selected articles and to segment these documents into clusters. Concurrently, the relationships between the identified items were examined. Furthermore, the keywords were analysed using the Word Cloud application. The remainder of this article is structured as shown. The Section 2 of the text provides a comprehensive explanation of the study design and the data source. The Section 3 of this study presents the results obtained from the analysis of the number of publications per year, the geographical distribution of studies by country, the word cloud analysis, the links between items, and the word networks.

## 2. Materials and Methods
### 2.1. Study Design
In recent years, the number of scientific contributions published by researchers in academic journals has increased [43]. These contributions are more frequently analysed using bibliometric methodologies [44,45,46,47]. Bibliometric analysis is a research methodology employed to study emerging trends in a specific area of scientific publications reported in well-known databases such as Scopus or Web of Science (WoS) [48]. Unlike qualitative methods, bibliometrics favours the objective statistical extrapolation of results from a scientific database, with less room for subjective bias. Indeed, bibliometric analysis can be used to analyse volume, distribution and growth trends within the extant literature, and has been identified as a quantitative method. Therefore, bibliometric analysis can be regarded as a scientific discipline involving quantitative and statistical analysis of the production, dissemination and utilisation of scientific knowledge [49]. In this review, a bibliometric analysis was conducted to study the literature in the field of aquaculture and circular economy. In particular, the study involved a performance analysis, quantitatively assessing the development of scientific publications over a ten-year period, the country of publication and the location where the experiments were conducted. This methodological approach facilitated mapping and identifying sub-themes underlying both aquaculture and the circular economy. The study used the Scopus database, a comprehensive resource well-suited to analysis [50]. Scopus is generally considered to be a more practical database than WoS thanks to its comprehensive authors, institutions and journal profiles, integrated interface, and more reliable impact indicators, which are available for all disciplines. Additionally, it is accessible as a single database without additional restrictions and offers free access to information on authors, journals and metrics. Some authors [51,52] observed that Scopus represents the database with higher journal coverage and faster citation analysis speed compared to the WoS database. It has also been observed that Scopus includes a greater number of documents and sources compared to WoS [53]. These characteristics led to the choice of Scopus instead of WoS. The search query focused on the Boolean combination of the two keywords (aquaculture) AND (circular economy), applied to several abstracts in order to select studies that deal with both topics.

## 2. Materials and Methods
### 2.1. Study Design
The search was limited to papers written in English and containing the keywords ‘aquaculture’ and ‘circular economy’ in their abstract, and to the subject areas ‘environmental sciences’, ‘agricultural and biological sciences’ and ‘economics, management and accounting’. The timeframe was set from 2015 to 2025 due to the need to prioritise the most current trends, particularly given the emergence of the circular economy as a significant scientific concept in the years following 2015 (Figure 1). Furthermore, the research was limited to ‘articles’ exclusively, with the aim of incorporating original and contemporary studies, providing detailed descriptions of circular economy practices in aquaculture that have been consolidated and studied by the scientific community.
**Figure 1.** Percentage of articles per year of publication.

## 2. Materials and Methods
### 2.2. Data Source
The Scopus database was selected for its ability to match bibliographic data with citation information, enabling analysis of the impact and trends of research [54]. The utilisation of sophisticated search systems encompassing systematic querying is a viable approach for identifying scientific publications. These systems allowed results to be refined based on criteria such as the year of publication, subject area, language, keywords, and article type, thereby ensuring a comprehensive and precise exploration of the extant literature [53]. In fact, Scopus and WoS are widely considered to be the most reliable databases for bibliographic research [53]. The Scopus bibliographic database was accessed on 29 May 2025 to minimise variations in the number of publications and citations. The first step involved data acquisition using the words ‘circular economy’ and ‘aquaculture’ in the field ‘search documents’; it resulted in the retrieval of 234 documents. The data obtained from the Scopus search was exported in MSExcel tabulated format, including bibliographic information such as titles, authors, journals, keywords and abstracts, as well as the year of publication. The keywords were then analysed using a word cloud. This method identifies recurring words by analysing their frequency of occurrence in the data entered into the programme [55]. The font size is directly proportional to the frequency with which the words occur, and different colours are used for each word [56]. The second phase involved the use of VOSviewer software (1.6.20, Nees Jan van Eck & Ludo Waltman, Centre for Science and Technology Studies, Leiden University, Leiden, The Netherlands) [42]. This bibliometric instrument incorporates methodologies for collaborative research and web-based analysis, encompassing key terms such as co-occurrence, bibliographic association, co-citation, and co-authorship [57]. Therefore, VOSviewer was used to map the selected articles by highlighting the main clusters based on bibliometric networks of the most frequently occurring words in the abstracts, and to obtain a graphical representation of the data [42,58]. The following criteria were used. The choice of the option ‘create a map based on textual data’ was dictated by the need to create a co-occurrence map of terms based on textual data. Subsequently, the option ‘read data from VOSviewer files’ was selected and the file analysed.

## 2. Materials and Methods
### 2.2. Data Source
The chosen counting method was ‘full counting’, to obtain the total number of occurrences of a term in each document. The terms were selected manually, considering a minimum occurrence of five. Then, using VOSviewer software, the links between the words were analysed, and co-occurrence networks were detected and visualised in maps.

## 3. Results
### 3.1. Bibliometric Analysis: Number of Publications per Year
Figure 1 reports the number of publications on aquaculture and the circular economy published each year. The results showed an absence of publications in the years 2015, 2016, 2017 and 2019 [59]. However, a descriptive analysis performed by [59] in the sustainable aquaculture sector revealed an increase in the volume of publications concerning aquaculture and the circular economy since 2020. Similar results were found by [60] in a mapping analysis of aquaculture research. Several factors promoted an increase in the number of published studies. Firstly, the increasing trend can be explained by heightened consumer awareness of environmentally damaging practices, which has prompted researchers to focus their studies on this issue. It is also interesting to observe the significant increase in publications after 2019 [61] (as shown in Figure 1), which may have been partly related to the onset of the coronavirus pandemic, which was influenced by climate change and intense human activity [62,63]. Indeed, as demonstrated by several researchers, pollution is one of the factors that contributed to the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 [64,65,66,67]. Therefore, the growing public awareness of the close interconnection between climate change, environmental pollution, and the pandemic significantly impacted risk perception [68,69], likely prompting researchers to conduct studies measuring sustainability in various food sectors [70,71,72,73,74,75]. Furthermore, the decline in consumption and trade and the subsequent production freeze may have stimulated innovation and promoted the development of circular economy models [38]. This increase may also have been encouraged by the publication of strategic reference frameworks for sustainable transitions, such as the 2030 Agenda and the European Green Deal.

## 3. Results
### 3.1. Bibliometric Analysis: Number of Publications per Year
The formulation of the 17 ‘Millennium Goals 2030’ issued by the UN in its 2015–2030 Agenda includes Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as number 14 (conserve and sustainably use the oceans), which includes Target 14.a ‘increase scientific knowledge, research, and marine and aquatic technology’; whereas the European Green Deal, published by the European Commission (EC) in 2019, defines policy initiatives for sustainable development by focusing attention on environmental protection. In addition, the development of digital technologies for implementation in aquaculture systems over the last ten years has promoted an increase in scientific research in this field [3,76]. This has resulted in increased attention and sensitivity to sustainable practices in the food sector, with a focus on aquaculture [59]. Consequently, the need for harmonised sustainable aquaculture practices among developed economies has been recognised [77,78,79]. This may have resulted in heightened awareness of environmental issues and, consequently, the necessity to prioritise sustainability and the circular economy in the aquaculture sector. The highest number of publications (25%) was found in 2024 (however, it should be considered that it is not yet 2025, and further studies may be published in the coming months). Overall, the selected studies mainly focus on exploiting by-products and residues from the fishing industry, innovative aquaponics strategies, and the possibility of purifying and reusing wastewater. Several studies focused on the reuse of mollusc shells [80], evaluating stakeholder opinion [80] and the shells’ potential to improve soil characteristics [81]. Finally, clam shells, following a low-temperature calcination process, were transformed into powder and coarse granules and used as soil improvers for the cultivation of clams [82]. Other studies aimed at the exploitation of fish waste as by-products of salicornia and tuna to produce feed for sea bass and fish hydrolysates, respectively [83,84]. The treatment of wastewater and sludge was also assessed before being introduced into these plants [85,86,87].

## 3. Results
### 3.1. Bibliometric Analysis: Number of Publications per Year
The studies published between 2018 and 2020 predominantly addressed conceptual and theoretical aspects, including life cycle assessment (LCA), green food protein (GFP) [88,89], characterisation of fish by-products [90], application of recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) [91], and assessment of the challenges and opportunities of working within a circular economy [92]. Therefore, these years functioned as a preparatory phase for subsequent applied experimentation. Since 2021, studies have started to focus on reusing agro-food by-products to feed fish and microalgae [93,94,95,96,97,98,99,100] producing innovative textiles [101], producing biodegradable compost from aquaculture [102], and treating antibiotic-contaminated water [103]. The first studies related to the valorisation of mollusc shells have been conducted since 2022 [104,105].

## 3. Results
### 3.4. Links Between Items
It has been shown that consuming approximately 2 g of omega-3 per week counteracts the risk of developing heart disease [148]. However, this correlation is indicative of a critical issue: the nutritional profile of fish is closely dependent on limited and unsustainable marine resources. Therefore, identifying valid alternatives to fishmeal would be optimal in order to achieve independence in terms of fish quality. The correlation between diet and fish meal items underscores the significance of selecting feed ingredients to achieve an optimal nutritional composition. Indeed, the correlation between dietary protein intake and the consumption of fish is indicative of the fish’s high protein content in the human diet. Fish provide approximately 20% of the protein consumed per capita by approximately 3.2 billion people [144]. Moreover, fish is made up of a high-quality protein that is highly digestible (over 90%) [149]. Indeed, a substantial correlation exists between aquaculture and protein items. Furthermore, considering the lower nutritional value of farmed fish compared to their wild counterparts, studies are underway to enhance the nutrient content of farmed fish in human diets [150]. Finally, the term ‘diet’ is closely associated with the word ‘salicornia’. This is due to their high protein content, n-3 and n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids and minerals [151,152], as well as the significant presence of bioactive secondary metabolites with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [151,153]. The correlations between the words that emerged from this analysis reflect the fact that the main challenge for the sector can be traced back to the transition towards feed with high nutritional value that meets sustainability requirements.
**Table 1.** Links between items.
**Figure 4.** Diet link; source: authors’ elaboration.
**Figure 5.** Fishmeal link; source: authors’ elaboration.

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
The map (Figure 6) and Table 2 developed by VOSviewer identify four word- clusters (coloured differently), with their respective coordinates and weights (e.g., occurrence, link, total link strength). Each cluster represents a different research area related to circularity practices in aquaculture. The proximity of words on a map suggests significant associations that emerge from their common usage within the same context. These associations can be used to identify the broad areas of research that characterise the current scientific literature on aquaculture. Table 2 shows the correspondence between clusters, respective words and scientific articles in which the words are present (numbered as shown in Table 1) and allows the articles to be attributed to each cluster. These articles are listed in the last column. Following this criterion, the four clusters were identified and named as follows:
**Figure 6.** Cluster networks on abstract; source: authors’ elaboration.

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
**Cluster 1**: By-products and effluent management represents the main group defined by a network (coloured in red in Figure 6) of eight words (compost, composting, energy, anaerobic digestion, organic matter, RAS, fish sludge and aquaponics). These words are primarily related to the management systems, processes and evaluation of the sustainability of aquaculture effluents, waste and fish sludge. The 25 articles collected in this cluster focus particularly on circular strategies for managing organic waste. Organic waste is considered to include fish sludge and organic matter compost [154]. Processes through which organic waste can be converted and valorised include anaerobic digestion [155,156,157], energy production through food loss, photovoltaic energy, CaO conversion of oyster, solar energy [90,92,125,126], RAS that allow the recovery of purified water, CO 2, and fish sludge [135,158,159], and aquaponics. The frequency of the term ‘compost’ and ‘composting’ indicates studies focusing on the production and use of compost in the agri-food sector. Indeed, some of the analysed studies focus on evaluating compost derived from aquaculture (e.g., shrimp aquaculture sludge, compost prepared with biodegradable waste from the aquaculture industry, liquid digestates from anaerobic digestion of food waste combined with fish sludge from recirculated aquaculture systems, composting process of RAS salmon sludge) processes to improve soil characteristics and plant growth [102,156,159,160]. Fish sludge was used as a raw material for producing energy and recovering nutrients [155]. Some authors [156] report the results of an assessment of the effect on the plant growth and on soil fertility from a circular economic perspective. In line with the recurrence of the term ‘aquaponics’, this cluster includes articles dealing with symbiotic aquaculture technologies. These combine the rearing of aquatic animals (carried out following the recirculating aquaculture system) with hydroponics, which consists of growing plants without soil. Aquaponics is one of the closed-loop circular techniques, alongside RAS and IMTA [161].

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
This technique can be defined as sustainable in nature [162,163], as it is based on a symbiotic cycle in which fish waste functions as a nutrient source for the plants. Concurrently, the latter facilitates the purification of the water present within the system, benefiting the fish. This approach promotes a closed-loop economy [164] which could be further made sustainable by using sensors and IoT technologies, with the advantage of monitoring fertilisation, irrigation and lighting [165,166,167]. The sustainability of aquaponics is related to:
(a)  
Water savings, achieved by conserving fresh water [168,169];
(b)  
The recycling of nutrients;
(c)  
The reduction in the use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides [170];
(d)  
The reduction in environmental impact;
(e)  
Urban and peri-urban adaptability;
(f)  
The use of conventional soil contaminants that are not relevant for crops [171].

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
The term ‘aquaponics’ is associated with the studies on this topic, including the use of wastewater from omega perch (Therapon barcoo) rearing for the hydroponic cultivation of cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.) [158], aquaponics-oriented ecopark design optimisation [157] and the evaluation of the growth of pitaya (Hylocereus spp.) cuttings in two aquaponic systems based on tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) rearing [172]. The anaerobic digestion process has been used to treat fish sludge in Norway and has been included in the design of eco-industrial parks [157]. The decision to categorise the first cluster as ‘Enhancement of by-products and effluents’ is also influenced by the inclusion of articles focusing on the valorisation of waste and by-products for fish feed replacement or soil fertilisers. BSFL raised on fish waste and corn grains from the distillery used for the partial replacement of fishmeal in fish feed for barramundi and sea bass are reported by [98,100,173]. The results from [173] highlighted how the total replacement of fishmeal with black soldier fly larval flour did not affect the nutritional value of the fish feed. In addition, ref. [81] reported on the evaluation of different treatments applied to mussel shells to produce fertilising powders that improve soil characteristics and fertility. The use of mussel shells as a soil improver can improve pH levels, the amount of organic matter, the available phosphorus and the exchangeable potassium. Other important approaches to aquaculture circularity covered by articles in this group include wastewater treatment and reuse technologies. In particular, the study by [103] presents the evaluation of magnetic composite materials consisting of waste biochar/titanium dioxide (BC/TiO 2) on the photodegradation of two antibiotics used in aquaculture. Ref. [158] deals with the recovery of wastewater deriving from breeding of omega/jade perch (Therapon barcoo) RAS for the hydroponic cultivation of cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.).

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
Another example of the opportunities represented by the recovery of brackish wastewater from fish farming is provided by article [136], which describes the use of wastewater from tilapia farming to cultivate microalgae. The cluster also includes several studies focusing on composting aquaculture sludge. Salmon farm sludge with a RAS has been used to recover nutrients and develop organic fertilisers for reuse in horticulture [86,159]. Furthermore, other studies have investigated the combined effect of fish sludge and liquid digestates, which result from the anaerobic digestion of food waste, on the propagation of plants such as Lepidium sativum and Triticum aestivum [156], in addition to analysing the growth of corn plants and soil in a Brazilian latosol following the addition of compost containing biodegradable waste resulting from the aquaculture process [102]. Nevertheless, the critical issues associated with regulating the cultivation of plant microalgae on composting sludge require further evaluation before the process can be transitioned from experimental studies to industrial-scale implementation.
This cluster emphasises the significance of waste treatment employed in aquaculture. Indeed, the optimal management of sustainability-oriented processes impacts the success of the business models adopted by companies, providing economic benefits for industry operators.

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
**Cluster 2**: Perception of sustainability and indicators in fish rearing systems: This cluster (coloured in green in Figure 6) was identified based on the frequency and links between the following words: BSFL (black soldier fly larvae), stakeholder, protein content, the supply chain, fishmeal and consumer. It includes 22 articles. Wild fish-based feed is the ideal feed in terms of nutritional completeness [174]; however, the high costs resulting from overfishing in recent years have led to the need to find new sources of raw materials and substitutes for fishmeal [148]. Finding suitable substitutes with a high protein content is the main challenge when replacing fishmeal with alternative feeds. Several studies focused on finding innovative, sustainable feed with an excellent nutritional profile [93,94,127,175]. The substantial focus on utilising black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens) in fish feed production is primarily due to their rich nutritional composition and amino acid profile. Secondly, this process has a significant potential to convert both food waste and manure into high-grade protein [176]. Numerous studies published in recent years underline the importance of this alternative fish feed ingredient [61,137,138,139,140,173,174,177,178]. These studies focus on using insect meal in aquaculture as part of a circular economy model aimed at creating a zero-waste society [61]. However, as the integration of insects into feed can elicit neophobic and disgust responses in consumers [179,180], studies on consumer acceptability must also be considered alongside those on nutritional benefits.

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
The presence of the term ‘stakeholder’ in the definition of the cluster highlights the importance of considering the opinions and perceptions of consumers, civil society and companies when evaluating the acceptability of any food or environmental-related innovation [181]. The successful implementation of innovations depends on several factors. Firstly, the ability to successfully transition processes from pilot to industrial experimental scale is essential. Secondly, the environmental performance of innovations needs to be measurable using suitable tools. Finally, social approval is a key factor. Indeed, it is well documented that neophobic stakeholder attitudes can create barriers to innovation implementation [182,183,184]. Indeed, the close connection between human and environmental health stems from the public’s increasing awareness of environmental impact and its growing demand for agro-food chains to become more sustainable [185,186]. The database includes studies based on the importance of stakeholders for a transaction towards more sustainable practices, the evaluation of perceptions of black soldier fly-based feed [88] and the acceptability of processes for the disposal and recovery of bivalve shells [80,139]. The term ‘supply chain’ is linked to the need for production chains to be managed efficiently, fairly and in an integrated way. This can be achieved by involving the various stakeholders and moving toward a circular economy approach to more sustainable processes [90]. Other studies included in this cluster evaluate methods for calculating the Green Protein Foodprint Index (GPF), which considers the environmental impact of a product and its protein content [89] and the combination of the nexus thinking approach with life cycle thinking [88]. Furthermore, ref. [187] studied the implementation of an innovative tool to analyse the sustainability of a production process considering the greening factor. The measurement was conducted in Chile and considered the five main firms of the aquaculture sector. Furthermore, a study was conducted based on the development of a methodology for a European multiregional input–output model for seafood, as well as an evaluation of the potential of this model [188] and an evaluation of the mathematical optimisation of fish protein hydrolysates derived from tuna waste [84]. Other studies investigated the acceptability of implementing a new approach to sustainable supply chain management. Ref. [189] analysed the implementation of blockchain technology in an integrated multitrophic aquaculture plant, considering both food and ornamental fish markets. Ref.

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
[80] evaluated a new model for the reuse of bivalve shells aimed at converting residues into innovative products considering sociocultural, economic and environmental aspects. For this purpose, a direct survey was conducted among stakeholders involved in both the production and consumption phases. The study highlighted the positive attitude of interested parties towards the proposed circular model, but also emphasised the need for comprehensive and detailed information on the proposed process to ensure effective acceptance and complete participation in the model. The recovery of shells from soil improvers may be of particular interest in terms of promoting circular economy development in coastal areas [80]. Ref. [139] investigated the willingness of interested parties to use black soldier fly larvae flour in Kenya. The risks and benefits perceived by interested parties were assessed, and the key issues related to legalisation and the advantages of promoting the use of BSFL in the fishing sector were identified. The findings of cluster 2 highlight the necessity for interconnection between technologies, sustainability metrics, governance support, and consumer consensus in developing innovative and widely applicable aquaculture systems. Therefore, the sustainable implementation of aquaculture systems should be aligned with current consumer needs.

This will involve carrying out a measurement of the circular practices applied in the relevant studies. A bibliometric analysis was conducted to identify the salient points of this field of research and potential future developments. The frequency with which articles on the subject were published from 2015 to 2025 was analysed. The authors’ affiliations were then considered to understand the geographical distribution of the studies and the places where the experiments were conducted. Furthermore, VOSviewer (VoS) software (version 1.6.20) [42] was utilised to identify a network of recurring words in the abstracts of the selected articles and to segment these documents into clusters. Concurrently, the relationships between the identified items were examined. Furthermore, the keywords were analysed using the Word Cloud application. The remainder of this article is structured as shown. The Section 2 of the text provides a comprehensive explanation of the study design and the data source. The Section 3 of this study presents the results obtained from the analysis of the number of publications per year, the geographical distribution of studies by country, the word cloud analysis, the links between items, and the word networks.

## 2. Materials and Methods
### 2.1. Study Design
In recent years, the number of scientific contributions published by researchers in academic journals has increased [43]. These contributions are more frequently analysed using bibliometric methodologies [44,45,46,47]. Bibliometric analysis is a research methodology employed to study emerging trends in a specific area of scientific publications reported in well-known databases such as Scopus or Web of Science (WoS) [48]. Unlike qualitative methods, bibliometrics favours the objective statistical extrapolation of results from a scientific database, with less room for subjective bias. Indeed, bibliometric analysis can be used to analyse volume, distribution and growth trends within the extant literature, and has been identified as a quantitative method. Therefore, bibliometric analysis can be regarded as a scientific discipline involving quantitative and statistical analysis of the production, dissemination and utilisation of scientific knowledge [49]. In this review, a bibliometric analysis was conducted to study the literature in the field of aquaculture and circular economy. In particular, the study involved a performance analysis, quantitatively assessing the development of scientific publications over a ten-year period, the country of publication and the location where the experiments were conducted. This methodological approach facilitated mapping and identifying sub-themes underlying both aquaculture and the circular economy. The study used the Scopus database, a comprehensive resource well-suited to analysis [50]. Scopus is generally considered to be a more practical database than WoS thanks to its comprehensive authors, institutions and journal profiles, integrated interface, and more reliable impact indicators, which are available for all disciplines. Additionally, it is accessible as a single database without additional restrictions and offers free access to information on authors, journals and metrics. Some authors [51,52] observed that Scopus represents the database with higher journal coverage and faster citation analysis speed compared to the WoS database. It has also been observed that Scopus includes a greater number of documents and sources compared to WoS [53]. These characteristics led to the choice of Scopus instead of WoS. The search query focused on the Boolean combination of the two keywords (aquaculture) AND (circular economy), applied to several abstracts in order to select studies that deal with both topics.

## 2. Materials and Methods
### 2.1. Study Design
The search was limited to papers written in English and containing the keywords ‘aquaculture’ and ‘circular economy’ in their abstract, and to the subject areas ‘environmental sciences’, ‘agricultural and biological sciences’ and ‘economics, management and accounting’. The timeframe was set from 2015 to 2025 due to the need to prioritise the most current trends, particularly given the emergence of the circular economy as a significant scientific concept in the years following 2015 (Figure 1). Furthermore, the research was limited to ‘articles’ exclusively, with the aim of incorporating original and contemporary studies, providing detailed descriptions of circular economy practices in aquaculture that have been consolidated and studied by the scientific community.
**Figure 1.** Percentage of articles per year of publication.
texts.10:
## 2. Materials and Methods
### 2.2. Data Source
The Scopus database was selected for its ability to match bibliographic data with citation information, enabling analysis of the impact and trends of research [54]. The utilisation of sophisticated search systems encompassing systematic querying is a viable approach for identifying scientific publications. These systems allowed results to be refined based on criteria such as the year of publication, subject area, language, keywords, and article type, thereby ensuring a comprehensive and precise exploration of the extant literature [53]. In fact, Scopus and WoS are widely considered to be the most reliable databases for bibliographic research [53]. The Scopus bibliographic database was accessed on 29 May 2025 to minimise variations in the number of publications and citations. The first step involved data acquisition using the words ‘circular economy’ and ‘aquaculture’ in the field ‘search documents’; it resulted in the retrieval of 234 documents. The data obtained from the Scopus search was exported in MSExcel tabulated format, including bibliographic information such as titles, authors, journals, keywords and abstracts, as well as the year of publication. The keywords were then analysed using a word cloud. This method identifies recurring words by analysing their frequency of occurrence in the data entered into the programme [55]. The font size is directly proportional to the frequency with which the words occur, and different colours are used for each word [56]. The second phase involved the use of VOSviewer software (1.6.20, Nees Jan van Eck & Ludo Waltman, Centre for Science and Technology Studies, Leiden University, Leiden, The Netherlands) [42]. This bibliometric instrument incorporates methodologies for collaborative research and web-based analysis, encompassing key terms such as co-occurrence, bibliographic association, co-citation, and co-authorship [57]. Therefore, VOSviewer was used to map the selected articles by highlighting the main clusters based on bibliometric networks of the most frequently occurring words in the abstracts, and to obtain a graphical representation of the data [42,58]. The following criteria were used. The choice of the option ‘create a map based on textual data’ was dictated by the need to create a co-occurrence map of terms based on textual data. Subsequently, the option ‘read data from VOSviewer files’ was selected and the file analysed.

## 2. Materials and Methods
### 2.2. Data Source
The chosen counting method was ‘full counting’, to obtain the total number of occurrences of a term in each document. The terms were selected manually, considering a minimum occurrence of five. Then, using VOSviewer software, the links between the words were analysed, and co-occurrence networks were detected and visualised in maps.

## 3. Results
### 3.1. Bibliometric Analysis: Number of Publications per Year
Figure 1 reports the number of publications on aquaculture and the circular economy published each year. The results showed an absence of publications in the years 2015, 2016, 2017 and 2019 [59]. However, a descriptive analysis performed by [59] in the sustainable aquaculture sector revealed an increase in the volume of publications concerning aquaculture and the circular economy since 2020. Similar results were found by [60] in a mapping analysis of aquaculture research. Several factors promoted an increase in the number of published studies. Firstly, the increasing trend can be explained by heightened consumer awareness of environmentally damaging practices, which has prompted researchers to focus their studies on this issue. It is also interesting to observe the significant increase in publications after 2019 [61] (as shown in Figure 1), which may have been partly related to the onset of the coronavirus pandemic, which was influenced by climate change and intense human activity [62,63]. Indeed, as demonstrated by several researchers, pollution is one of the factors that contributed to the transmission of SARS-CoV-2 [64,65,66,67]. Therefore, the growing public awareness of the close interconnection between climate change, environmental pollution, and the pandemic significantly impacted risk perception [68,69], likely prompting researchers to conduct studies measuring sustainability in various food sectors [70,71,72,73,74,75]. Furthermore, the decline in consumption and trade and the subsequent production freeze may have stimulated innovation and promoted the development of circular economy models [38]. This increase may also have been encouraged by the publication of strategic reference frameworks for sustainable transitions, such as the 2030 Agenda and the European Green Deal.
texts.13:
## 3. Results
### 3.1. Bibliometric Analysis: Number of Publications per Year
The formulation of the 17 ‘Millennium Goals 2030’ issued by the UN in its 2015–2030 Agenda includes Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), such as number 14 (conserve and sustainably use the oceans), which includes Target 14.a ‘increase scientific knowledge, research, and marine and aquatic technology’; whereas the European Green Deal, published by the European Commission (EC) in 2019, defines policy initiatives for sustainable development by focusing attention on environmental protection. In addition, the development of digital technologies for implementation in aquaculture systems over the last ten years has promoted an increase in scientific research in this field [3,76]. This has resulted in increased attention and sensitivity to sustainable practices in the food sector, with a focus on aquaculture [59]. Consequently, the need for harmonised sustainable aquaculture practices among developed economies has been recognised [77,78,79]. This may have resulted in heightened awareness of environmental issues and, consequently, the necessity to prioritise sustainability and the circular economy in the aquaculture sector. The highest number of publications (25%) was found in 2024 (however, it should be considered that it is not yet 2025, and further studies may be published in the coming months). Overall, the selected studies mainly focus on exploiting by-products and residues from the fishing industry, innovative aquaponics strategies, and the possibility of purifying and reusing wastewater. Several studies focused on the reuse of mollusc shells [80], evaluating stakeholder opinion [80] and the shells’ potential to improve soil characteristics [81]. Finally, clam shells, following a low-temperature calcination process, were transformed into powder and coarse granules and used as soil improvers for the cultivation of clams [82]. Other studies aimed at the exploitation of fish waste as by-products of salicornia and tuna to produce feed for sea bass and fish hydrolysates, respectively [83,84]. The treatment of wastewater and sludge was also assessed before being introduced into these plants [85,86,87].
texts.14:
## 3. Results
### 3.1. Bibliometric Analysis: Number of Publications per Year
The studies published between 2018 and 2020 predominantly addressed conceptual and theoretical aspects, including life cycle assessment (LCA), green food protein (GFP) [88,89], characterisation of fish by-products [90], application of recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS) [91], and assessment of the challenges and opportunities of working within a circular economy [92]. Therefore, these years functioned as a preparatory phase for subsequent applied experimentation. Since 2021, studies have started to focus on reusing agro-food by-products to feed fish and microalgae [93,94,95,96,97,98,99,100] producing innovative textiles [101], producing biodegradable compost from aquaculture [102], and treating antibiotic-contaminated water [103]. The first studies related to the valorisation of mollusc shells have been conducted since 2022 [104,105].

## 3. Results
### 3.4. Links Between Items
It has been shown that consuming approximately 2 g of omega-3 per week counteracts the risk of developing heart disease [148]. However, this correlation is indicative of a critical issue: the nutritional profile of fish is closely dependent on limited and unsustainable marine resources. Therefore, identifying valid alternatives to fishmeal would be optimal in order to achieve independence in terms of fish quality. The correlation between diet and fish meal items underscores the significance of selecting feed ingredients to achieve an optimal nutritional composition. Indeed, the correlation between dietary protein intake and the consumption of fish is indicative of the fish’s high protein content in the human diet. Fish provide approximately 20% of the protein consumed per capita by approximately 3.2 billion people [144]. Moreover, fish is made up of a high-quality protein that is highly digestible (over 90%) [149]. Indeed, a substantial correlation exists between aquaculture and protein items. Furthermore, considering the lower nutritional value of farmed fish compared to their wild counterparts, studies are underway to enhance the nutrient content of farmed fish in human diets [150]. Finally, the term ‘diet’ is closely associated with the word ‘salicornia’. This is due to their high protein content, n-3 and n-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids and minerals [151,152], as well as the significant presence of bioactive secondary metabolites with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [151,153]. The correlations between the words that emerged from this analysis reflect the fact that the main challenge for the sector can be traced back to the transition towards feed with high nutritional value that meets sustainability requirements.

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
The map (Figure 6) and Table 2 developed by VOSviewer identify four word- clusters (coloured differently), with their respective coordinates and weights (e.g., occurrence, link, total link strength). Each cluster represents a different research area related to circularity practices in aquaculture. The proximity of words on a map suggests significant associations that emerge from their common usage within the same context. These associations can be used to identify the broad areas of research that characterise the current scientific literature on aquaculture. Table 2 shows the correspondence between clusters, respective words and scientific articles in which the words are present (numbered as shown in Table 1) and allows the articles to be attributed to each cluster. These articles are listed in the last column. Following this criterion, the four clusters were identified and named as follows:

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
**Cluster 1**: By-products and effluent management represents the main group defined by a network (coloured in red in Figure 6) of eight words (compost, composting, energy, anaerobic digestion, organic matter, RAS, fish sludge and aquaponics). These words are primarily related to the management systems, processes and evaluation of the sustainability of aquaculture effluents, waste and fish sludge. The 25 articles collected in this cluster focus particularly on circular strategies for managing organic waste. Organic waste is considered to include fish sludge and organic matter compost [154]. Processes through which organic waste can be converted and valorised include anaerobic digestion [155,156,157], energy production through food loss, photovoltaic energy, CaO conversion of oyster, solar energy [90,92,125,126], RAS that allow the recovery of purified water, CO 2, and fish sludge [135,158,159], and aquaponics. The frequency of the term ‘compost’ and ‘composting’ indicates studies focusing on the production and use of compost in the agri-food sector. Indeed, some of the analysed studies focus on evaluating compost derived from aquaculture (e.g., shrimp aquaculture sludge, compost prepared with biodegradable waste from the aquaculture industry, liquid digestates from anaerobic digestion of food waste combined with fish sludge from recirculated aquaculture systems, composting process of RAS salmon sludge) processes to improve soil characteristics and plant growth [102,156,159,160]. Fish sludge was used as a raw material for producing energy and recovering nutrients [155]. Some authors [156] report the results of an assessment of the effect on the plant growth and on soil fertility from a circular economic perspective. In line with the recurrence of the term ‘aquaponics’, this cluster includes articles dealing with symbiotic aquaculture technologies. These combine the rearing of aquatic animals (carried out following the recirculating aquaculture system) with hydroponics, which consists of growing plants without soil. Aquaponics is one of the closed-loop circular techniques, alongside RAS and IMTA [161].
texts.25:
## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
The term ‘aquaponics’ is associated with the studies on this topic, including the use of wastewater from omega perch (Therapon barcoo) rearing for the hydroponic cultivation of cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.) [158], aquaponics-oriented ecopark design optimisation [157] and the evaluation of the growth of pitaya (Hylocereus spp.) cuttings in two aquaponic systems based on tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus) rearing [172]. The anaerobic digestion process has been used to treat fish sludge in Norway and has been included in the design of eco-industrial parks [157]. The decision to categorise the first cluster as ‘Enhancement of by-products and effluents’ is also influenced by the inclusion of articles focusing on the valorisation of waste and by-products for fish feed replacement or soil fertilisers. BSFL raised on fish waste and corn grains from the distillery used for the partial replacement of fishmeal in fish feed for barramundi and sea bass are reported by [98,100,173]. The results from [173] highlighted how the total replacement of fishmeal with black soldier fly larval flour did not affect the nutritional value of the fish feed. In addition, ref. [81] reported on the evaluation of different treatments applied to mussel shells to produce fertilising powders that improve soil characteristics and fertility. The use of mussel shells as a soil improver can improve pH levels, the amount of organic matter, the available phosphorus and the exchangeable potassium. Other important approaches to aquaculture circularity covered by articles in this group include wastewater treatment and reuse technologies. In particular, the study by [103] presents the evaluation of magnetic composite materials consisting of waste biochar/titanium dioxide (BC/TiO 2) on the photodegradation of two antibiotics used in aquaculture. Ref. [158] deals with the recovery of wastewater deriving from breeding of omega/jade perch (Therapon barcoo) RAS for the hydroponic cultivation of cucumber (Cucumis sativus L.).
texts.26:
## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
Another example of the opportunities represented by the recovery of brackish wastewater from fish farming is provided by article [136], which describes the use of wastewater from tilapia farming to cultivate microalgae. The cluster also includes several studies focusing on composting aquaculture sludge. Salmon farm sludge with a RAS has been used to recover nutrients and develop organic fertilisers for reuse in horticulture [86,159]. Furthermore, other studies have investigated the combined effect of fish sludge and liquid digestates, which result from the anaerobic digestion of food waste, on the propagation of plants such as Lepidium sativum and Triticum aestivum [156], in addition to analysing the growth of corn plants and soil in a Brazilian latosol following the addition of compost containing biodegradable waste resulting from the aquaculture process [102]. Nevertheless, the critical issues associated with regulating the cultivation of plant microalgae on composting sludge require further evaluation before the process can be transitioned from experimental studies to industrial-scale implementation.
This cluster emphasises the significance of waste treatment employed in aquaculture. Indeed, the optimal management of sustainability-oriented processes impacts the success of the business models adopted by companies, providing economic benefits for industry operators.
texts.27:
## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
**Cluster 2**: Perception of sustainability and indicators in fish rearing systems: This cluster (coloured in green in Figure 6) was identified based on the frequency and links between the following words: BSFL (black soldier fly larvae), stakeholder, protein content, the supply chain, fishmeal and consumer. It includes 22 articles. Wild fish-based feed is the ideal feed in terms of nutritional completeness [174]; however, the high costs resulting from overfishing in recent years have led to the need to find new sources of raw materials and substitutes for fishmeal [148]. Finding suitable substitutes with a high protein content is the main challenge when replacing fishmeal with alternative feeds. Several studies focused on finding innovative, sustainable feed with an excellent nutritional profile [93,94,127,175]. The substantial focus on utilising black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens) in fish feed production is primarily due to their rich nutritional composition and amino acid profile. Secondly, this process has a significant potential to convert both food waste and manure into high-grade protein [176]. Numerous studies published in recent years underline the importance of this alternative fish feed ingredient [61,137,138,139,140,173,174,177,178]. These studies focus on using insect meal in aquaculture as part of a circular economy model aimed at creating a zero-waste society [61]. However, as the integration of insects into feed can elicit neophobic and disgust responses in consumers [179,180], studies on consumer acceptability must also be considered alongside those on nutritional benefits.

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
The presence of the term ‘stakeholder’ in the definition of the cluster highlights the importance of considering the opinions and perceptions of consumers, civil society and companies when evaluating the acceptability of any food or environmental-related innovation [181]. The successful implementation of innovations depends on several factors. Firstly, the ability to successfully transition processes from pilot to industrial experimental scale is essential. Secondly, the environmental performance of innovations needs to be measurable using suitable tools. Finally, social approval is a key factor. Indeed, it is well documented that neophobic stakeholder attitudes can create barriers to innovation implementation [182,183,184]. Indeed, the close connection between human and environmental health stems from the public’s increasing awareness of environmental impact and its growing demand for agro-food chains to become more sustainable [185,186]. The database includes studies based on the importance of stakeholders for a transaction towards more sustainable practices, the evaluation of perceptions of black soldier fly-based feed [88] and the acceptability of processes for the disposal and recovery of bivalve shells [80,139]. The term ‘supply chain’ is linked to the need for production chains to be managed efficiently, fairly and in an integrated way. This can be achieved by involving the various stakeholders and moving toward a circular economy approach to more sustainable processes [90]. Other studies included in this cluster evaluate methods for calculating the Green Protein Foodprint Index (GPF), which considers the environmental impact of a product and its protein content [89] and the combination of the nexus thinking approach with life cycle thinking [88]. Furthermore, ref. [187] studied the implementation of an innovative tool to analyse the sustainability of a production process considering the greening factor. The measurement was conducted in Chile and considered the five main firms of the aquaculture sector. Furthermore, a study was conducted based on the development of a methodology for a European multiregional input–output model for seafood, as well as an evaluation of the potential of this model [188] and an evaluation of the mathematical optimisation of fish protein hydrolysates derived from tuna waste [84]. Other studies investigated the acceptability of implementing a new approach to sustainable supply chain management. Ref. [189] analysed the implementation of blockchain technology in an integrated multitrophic aquaculture plant, considering both food and ornamental fish markets. Ref.

## 3. Results
### 3.5. Word Networks
[80] evaluated a new model for the reuse of bivalve shells aimed at converting residues into innovative products considering sociocultural, economic and environmental aspects. For this purpose, a direct survey was conducted among stakeholders involved in both the production and consumption phases. The study highlighted the positive attitude of interested parties towards the proposed circular model, but also emphasised the need for comprehensive and detailed information on the proposed process to ensure effective acceptance and complete participation in the model. The recovery of shells from soil improvers may be of particular interest in terms of promoting circular economy development in coastal areas [80]. Ref. [139] investigated the willingness of interested parties to use black soldier fly larvae flour in Kenya. The risks and benefits perceived by interested parties were assessed, and the key issues related to legalisation and the advantages of promoting the use of BSFL in the fishing sector were identified. The findings of cluster 2 highlight the necessity for interconnection between technologies, sustainability metrics, governance support, and consumer consensus in developing innovative and widely applicable aquaculture systems. Therefore, the sustainable implementation of aquaculture systems should be aligned with current consumer needs.
